paper_title: ChARM Character-based Act-adaptive Reward Modeling for Advanced   Role-Playing Language Agents
caption: The character distribution in RoleplayPref consists of 3 primary categories and 13 subcategories.

model_annotations.Bulgarian: The diagram illustrates the character distribution in RoleplayPref, organized into three primary categories—Virtual Characters, Real Characters, and Custom Characters—further subdivided into 13 distinct subcategories. The largest segment, “Virtual Characters,” occupies the majority of the inner circle and is colored light blue, encompassing five subcategories: Comic Characters, Movie Characters, Teleplay Characters, Novel Characters, and Game Characters, each represented as equal-sized segments in the outer ring. The “Real Characters” category, shown in green, is subdivided into six subcategories: Scientists, Artists, Athletes, Writers, Musicians, and Actors, with Influencers appearing as a separate but visually connected segment; these segments vary slightly in size but are generally smaller than those under Virtual Characters. The “Custom Characters” category, depicted in pink, is a single, relatively small segment. The diagram uses a concentric ring layout with no numerical percentages displayed, and no segment is visually emphasized through separation or highlighting; the subcategories are arranged in a clockwise order around the central categories, with no explicit indication of proportional weighting beyond visual size. A legend is not present, and all labels are placed adjacent to their respective segments.
model_annotations.English: The pie chart illustrates the character distribution in the RoleplayPref dataset, organized into three primary categories—Virtual Characters, Real Characters, and Custom Characters—each subdivided into specific subcategories. The largest segment, Virtual Characters (light blue), encompasses five subcategories: Comic Characters, Movie Characters, Teleplay Characters, Novel Characters, and Game Characters, collectively occupying the majority of the chart. Real Characters (light green) include seven subcategories: Scientists, Artists, Athletes, Writers, Musicians, Actors, and Influencers, forming a moderately sized portion. Custom Characters (light pink) represent the smallest segment, with no further subdivisions shown. The chart uses distinct pastel colors for each primary category and its subcategories, with labels placed radially outside the pie. While percentages are not numerically labeled, the visual proportions suggest Virtual Characters dominate, followed by Real Characters, with Custom Characters comprising the smallest share. The structure reflects a hierarchical breakdown of character types used in role-playing language agent training, as referenced in the paper “ChARM: Character-based Act-adaptive Reward Modeling for Advanced Role-Playing Language Agents.”

The Real Characters category, shown in green, is segmented into seven subcategories: Scientists, Artists, Athletes, Writers, Musicians, Actors, and Influencers, with each subcategory represented by a distinct shade of green and arranged in a clockwise sequence. The Custom Characters category, depicted in pink, constitutes a single segment without further subdivision. The chart uses a central hole to emphasize the categorical breakdown, with labels placed outside the ring for clarity; no numerical percentages are displayed, and segments are ordered clockwise starting from the top.
